p: Yeah. And to the mayor’s office, Ms. Wisdom, is part of what you’re trying to do to put more resources into prevention, into doing education? We’ve heard now both from the NYPD and the DAs office that that kind of education seemed to be effective tools in preventing these kind of hate crimes.

Yes, absolutely. Thank you for the question. We don’t have a specific budget proposals or program or policy proposals for this budget cycle, because we’re mid-budget cycle. But absolutely want to follow through on the mayor's commitment to increase funding to hate crime prevention.

I mean, I know we’ve seen the Speaker, we’ve talked about it, and Council Member Brewer raised this earlier, beginning

to talk about the Holocaust and trying to do real education out there around antisemitism. Is there a commitment from the mayor’s office to look for additional resources to do the education that we’re talking about, whether to the DA, NYPD or through your office?
Yes, absolutely.

And what would you need from the Council to advance, or what structural support with the mayor’s office need to make sure that we’re saying the same thing? Because clearly– I know the Speaker’s talked a lot about prevention, you know. What else do you need from us to do to ensure that prevention is happening– resources are happening?

I think primarily to keep in touch with each other about what we’re hearing from communities, what they need, and then there will be budgetary asks most likely next year that will be coming to the council floor to talk about.

Yeah, we’d love to see something this year, obviously, because we

don’t want to— you know, obviously, people who get, you know, injured, harmed by hate crimes. We want to get in front of this as much as possible. Whatever we can do collectively to ensure there are resources in place whether through the DAs office or through the NYPD, with your office to that kind of prevention, I think it really goes a long way in drawing with the underlying problems we’ve seen over the rise of antisemitism. I want to thank the co-chairs for letting me ask again.
Thank you, Council Member. We actually have no further questions for DA Gonzalez. You’re free to stay, but– if you wish. Thank you very much for being here.
Thank you, Chairs, and thank you, Council Member Epstein.

Alright. I have some– I have some questions for the NYPD. Just following up on Council Member Dinowitz’s question about your training, could you tell us a little bit about what materials you use for training?
We can certainly provide you with the curriculum.
Please. Thank you. What is the headcount in your Hate Crimes Unit, if you have it?
Yes, the current headcount of the Hate Crime Taskforce is 25 uniformed members of the service, and that is inclusive of 20 total detectives that investigate cases.
Is that– do you find that sufficient?
We do.

Okay. Can you talk a little bit about how the NYPD defines– I know you spoke about how you define hate crimes. You follow the penal law. But what about antisemitic hate crimes and how do you define antisemitism, and what if any guidelines you use for that definition?

Alright. So, we’re coming back really to the state statute, and we’re not using– we’re not using some free-standing definition of antisemitism. Other words, the legal question that we’re answering as a matter of state law is under the hate crimes statute was– and again, this is a paraphrase, but this is the concept, right? Was this person a victim in whole or

in substantial part because that person was Jewish or perceived to be Jewish, right? That is the question. That is the question– the legal question that has to be answered. We have probable cause supporting that. And that's the question we’re answering. So, there's no sort of free-standing definition of antisemitism that we’re applying or really in any of these bias categories some sort of free-standing definition. We’re – in each case we’re saying, okay, this is the protected characteristic. Here– Judaism is Jewish, and then we’re answering that legal question under state law.
So, we’re not following any specific definition? For example, our definition is used quite often. Are you saying just case by case basis?

No, no, no. I’m not saying case by case. What I’m saying is that this is a state law question. In other words, we can’t just sort of unilaterally decide oh, we're going to pick up everything from antisemitism and apply that to the New York State hate crimes law, right? LIke, we– that’s a state law. The state legislature says, okay here’s how we’re defining a

hate crime, right? And the way that it’s defined under state law is, again as I said, it’s penal law and it’s 45.05. Again, in whole or substantial part, because of– and then it lists the various characteristics. So, we’re obligated to follow state law.
So, how do– just so I’m clear, how do we know if something is an antisemitic hate crime?

So, that’s what the investigation is, right? So, we talk about like bias, right? Was this because, in whole or in part, because the person was Jewish or perceived to be Jewish. That’s the question the detectives are trying to answer, right? Again, take the example of someone who’s punched in the face. Did that happen in whole or in substantial part because the attacker had a belief or perception about their being Jewish, perception that they Jewish? If that’s why this happeneing– that’s why this happened, now we’re talking about a hate crime.

Okay. We can explore more a little bit later on. I want to ask

you, has the Mayor’s Office of Antisemitism reached out to you?

So, I mean, I’ve spoken with the Executive Director on multiple occasions. I think we actually had our meeting– an in-person meeting scheduled– I’m not sure exactly when. It’s coming up. But yeah, so I have obviously– I spoke with the Executive Director, and we’re going to have in-person meetings as well.
And I assume antisemitic hate crimes are on the agenda.
Absolutely.
Thank you. Can you talk a little bit about how the NYPD Hate Crimes Taskforce determination process works when it comes to hate crimes and bias incidents?
Well–
Like, what happens after a person reports a hate crime–

[interposing] Right, so you have the investigation that’s done. And again, what’s interesting about these investigations is because of the really unique nature of a hate crime, it’s not just the crime itself that’s being

investigated, though that is done in an incredibly thorough and deliberate way, but also if there’s other evidence that goes to the perpetrator’s motivation, right? So, they’re– the taskforce is gathering all that evidence, doing all that work. The determinate– as a formal matter, as a formal matter the determination if something is or is not a confirmed hate crime is made by the commanding officer of the Hate Crimes Taskforce. That is very much in consultation with the Legal Bureau, and again, we have a lawyer assigned over there. And to be blunt, there are some cases that are totally obvious, right, that they’re not going to need to talk to legal, because it’s plain as day that it’s anti-Jewish or antisemitic in nature and we can prove it.
Could you give an example of a case that’s totally obvious?
Yeah. Somebody walks up to someone. The person is visibly Jewish. Is saying antisemitic slurs and punches that person in the face.
Could you give an example of an antisemitic slur?
I– I mean, if calling some one let’s say a kike. I think that’s a pretty, you know, antisemitic slur.

Thank you. How many– I think you answered this question before, so I’ll just move on. While Jewish New Yorkers make up roughly 10 percent of the city’s population, they were targeted in over half of all confirmed hate crimes in the first quarter of 26. If you know, to what does the NYPD attribute this disproportionate targeting of Jewish New Yorkers?

As I was saying before, it’s– antisemitism generally– I mean, it’s– this goes back a question across time and the world and millennia and trying to understand and articulate why there’s hatred for the Jews, you know, in particular hatred for the Jews that is disproportionate to other hatreds out there in the world, right? It’s a very hard question to answer.
I understand that.

I think there’s that constant– there’s a constant, right, in history, and then the question becomes okay, to what extent do– you know, for example, world events affect

hate crimes here in New York City. As I said before, you know, certainly as an intuitive matter, I would think so. We see it in the data post October 7th clear as day. Beyond that, I’m not sure I can tell you in a definite way, oh, you know– hard to draw a line sometimes. Between something, a world event and antisemitic hate crime activity in New York City, but– you know, and to the DA’s point, with everything going on in social media, things can happen around the world and have an effect here on crime in New York City.
Okay. Does the Department receive written guidance from any of the five District Attorneys or from any of them jointly on what conduct is or is not chargeable as a hate crime under penal law 4505?

So, I– we will check. I don’t think there's anything like a formal memo the way– I mean– I want to emphasize this, though, we are in regular contact with the DA’s office generally, but in particular when it comes to Hate Crimes Taskforce. We are talking to the DA’s offices and the US Attorney’s offices all the time. It is a very, very collaborative, productive

relationship. And so, you know, just to really speak to what you’re getting at, I think our detectives and the leadership of the Hate Crimes Taskforce, we have to make our own determinations, of course. There’ll be times when we and the DA’s office disagree. That can happen and that’s okay, but I think we have a good sense, for all the DA’s offices, of how they think about these things.
So, no written guidance exists, is that correct?
Certainly not that I’m aware of. We will double-check, but I don’t think so.
Please, if you could double-check. I mean, if there isn’t any, could you confirm that to us in writing?
Sure.

thank you very much. When the Hate Crimes Taskforce is building a case that involves difficult classification questions, for example zionist slogan directed at a visibly Jewish victim, is there a practice of consulting the relevant DAs before arrest?

So, I would say there’s very, very often conversations in these types of situations. So yes, there’s very often dialogue. I don’t want to say that– I don’t want to commit to that it happens 100 percent of the time, right? But yes, there is regular dialogue with the DAs, particularly in the– in more– it’s an open question. There will regularly be contact with the DAs, yes.

Okay. And when the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office, which happens often, declines to take a hate crime case referred by the Department or declines to include the hate crime enhancement in his charging, does the Department receive an explanation, whether in writing or not in writing?
Without specificity, I can answer it anecdotally, and I can tell you–
[interposing] I’m sorry. Can you repeat that?

I’m so sorry. Without specificity to a specific case, I can answer it anecdotally and talk about the protocols and the

methodology by which the detectives and their supervisors and commanding officer of Hate Crimes Taskforce deals with things like that. Those are conversations that are certainly had between the commanding officer of the Hate Crime Taskforce, the attorney assigned to the Hate Crime Taskforce, and the prosecutor from the DA’s office, and if there’s a divergence of opinion, we have those conversations, and we note them, and we as the NYPD go forward with what we perceive the charge to be.
How can we get a copy of those notes?

Actually, to be blunt, those notes, the deliberations over particular cases, internal deliberations whether within the NYPD or with the DA’s offices, I actually do not think that is something, respectfully, that should be going out really to the City Council or the public. I mean, those are really important discussions that we need to have. They’re really important and they have to be candid discussions. They have to be very blunt, right? Blunt on both ends, that we can be candid about our view on a case. DA’s office, blunt on their view. And by the way,

that could be strengths and weaknesses of a case. Sometimes the disagreements could be legal in nature. Sometimes, how strong is the evidence, right? We might think the case is strong. They have a concern about a witness. Those are very, very sensitive discussions that have to be done with candor. You know, to the extent that those discussions are not going to be shared with the public, that’s going to actually have a really adverse effect on our ability to successfully bring these cases.

I would still request that you provide us with a redacted copy of– let’s say from 2025 and as it relates to Manhattan District Attorney’s office specifically. And if you really can’t provide, I guess just let us know in writing.
And I also– Council Member, I just want to be clear. It’s not like– I don’t even know if there are notes. What I mean is–
[interposing] No, I mean, you just testified that notes being taken.

No, I said– no, there are conversations that are had. There are

conversations that are had. Whether or not notes were taken, I have no idea. And again, like it’s not like there’s some form that’s filled out in each case and like our view, the DA’s office’s view. It’s going to range tremendously, right? You could have some case where there are multiple conversations. Somewhere there’s one, it’s long, it’s short. These internal sorts of deliberations, again, that we’re to be able to have them with candor. And in a world in which that's going to be shared publicly, it’s going to make it much more difficult for us to work with the DA’s office and for the DA’s office to work with us. We have to be able to speak just very bluntly with each other about the particulars of cases.

I still request the redacted notes if possible, and again, if you can’t provide it, just let us know in writing if possible. Thank you. Let’s talk a little bit about the reporting changes that were made. As we discussed here, there were recent reports about changes and how NYPD reports hate crimes. I know you explained some of the changes. Were these changes made exclusively by the NYPD, or was this decision from the administration broadly?
There were decisions by the NYPD. We made these decisions. We stand by them. These were not decisions made by anyone at City Hall. We made these decisions.
And was the mayor’s office consulted in any way on those decisions?

Not consulted with. Before we announced the decisions– and again, we announced them twice, right? There was once– one announcement at the beginning of March, one at the beginning of April. Before those announcements were made, we informed City Hall we would be making those announcements. But to be blunt, it was not– we had made the decision. We were going to announce it. We let City Hall know.
So, is it accurate to say that NYPD can make decisions without the Mayor’s input?

So, we made decisions every day on a wide range of matters. Some of them, right, are very much in consultation with City Hall, and then the NYPD, so much going on. There are many, many things that we decide without input from City Hall, and you know, there are

judgement calls about what is raised and discussed and what isn’t. I just want to be very, very clear on these issues. These were decisions that we made ourselves.
Okay, thank you. And was the Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism consulted or–
[interposing] No, no.
advised?
Again, very shortly began we made each of these announcements, we notified, we told City Hall, hey we’re about to announce facts [sic].

Okay, thank you. During the weeks the Department was publishing only confirmed figures, can you tell us approximately how many incidents– if you have the information. If not, you could provide it to us at a later time. How many incidents were under investigation as possible hate crimes that did not appear in the public [inaudible].

So, you’re– so, if what you’re asking for– I think– so let’s say, going back, we only have the confirmed hate crime

numbers. We were not tracking in a systematic way all possible, all reported hate crimes. In other words, what we’re doing now, and again we’re tracking this quite carefully. We’re pouring it out monthly– is both the full universe of cases that are being investigated by the taskforce and the full universe of confirmed hate crimes by the taskforce. What weren’t tracking before in a way that we’d be comfortable reporting out on is the full universe of just the incoming to the taskforce. So, I’m not sure I could answer your question, because the whole point is that wasn’t data we were tracking before. We are now tracking and reporting on that going forward.
I think you’ve answered the things. Are the reported hate crimes listed separately from the confirmed hate crimes, or just like talk to us a little bit about how–

[interposing] Sure. so, going forward monthly, and you saw this in the– you saw this this month when we report on our March crime numbers. We provided– we actually provided three things. We provided the confirmed hate crimes numbers for March. Because it’s the quarter, we gave the confirmed hate crimes number for

the quarter [inaudible] and then separately was the universe for March of all reported hate crimes broken down by the type of bias.
That’s every crime that was reported during that period of time, correct?
For a monthly basis, that’s every case that is coming into the Hate Crimes Taskforce.
Okay. And can you talk a little bit more about what it means to have a confirmed hate crime?

Right. So, confirmed hate crime is really that legal determination we’re talking about saying under the statute, we believe we have probable cause that this is a hate crime pursuant to 45.05. That’s what a confirmed hate crime is.
And who makes that determination?
The CO of the Hate Crimes Taskforce, and again, if necessary in consultation with the Legal Bureau.
And what happens if the victim chooses not to press charges?
So, it–
[interposing] Is that then considered just a reported hate crime or is that confirmed in some way?

So, the analysis of whether something’s a confirmed hate crime is going to be separate and apart from whether or not the person wants to go forward. We can have a confirmed hate crime. The victim can say, hey, I don’t want to proceed with this. We then have to assess whether we’ll be able to make our case, right?
That’s why I’m asking.

It’ll be a confirmed hate crime, yes. There certainly could be scenarios, like hypotheticals where it’s a confirmed hate crime. [inaudible] the victim chooses not to go forward, which is, you know, that person’s right. But we would still have it a confirmed hate crime.

Okay, got it. Comes to the public reporting of hate crimes– oh, I’m sorry, I asked this question. Are there crimes

reported in the same way that hate crimes are currently? Like sexual assault, for example. Is that reported in the same way as hate crimes?

No. I mean, we– our reporting on hate crimes is unique in that we have these both– sort of these two levels, right? The incoming of the taskforce and the confirmed hate crimes number. We trade– and we have the dashboard and all that. We don't have this for every type of crime. We treat hate crimes differently because of the unique nature of the crime, because as we’ve been discussing, it’s a crime not only– it’s harm on a victim, but to communities, the effect it has on society. The fact that the state chooses to treat hate crimes differently than other types of crimes–
[interposing] I mean, I would argue that sexual assault is also a crime of unique nature.
Of course.
So, why is that reported differently than a hate crime?

Because what you– the issue is, and this goes back to what DA Gonzalez was referring to. You have these two steps

with a hate crime, right? It’s the criminal activity itself, and then the question, whether you can prove the motive, right? So, everything we’re talking about here with hate crimes, it’s a two-level thing. That’s separate and apart from the complaint coming in, right? In other words, the per– the situation where someone’s assaulted, and the question was can you prove that it was a hate crime? It was, you know, anti-Jewish in nature. In which way, that assault is going to be recorded. It’s an assault, right? That complaint has been taken. That’s going to be in our data as an assault in whatever the appropriate degree is. So, that’s the analog to every other type of crime. The crime comes in. It's recorded, right? And then we see whether we can catch the perpetrator. You have this separate question for hate crimes about motive, whether we can prove it. As the DA said, that is actually unique to hate crimes in what you have is a two-layers of reporting.
So, the difference is due to the motives?

The need to establish motive. Because there are two separate

questions, right? One, as with anything, okay, is there a crime here? Right? And that’s true for anything under the sun. Is there a crime? And then there’s a separate issue, right, of can we show that the person’s motive was bias-based. And that is really– that’s unique. It’s unique for hate crimes. Other types of crimes, we don’t care what your motive was. You committed a crime. If we can prove that you did it, you’re going to get arrested. But for hate crimes, to charge as a hate crime, the separate special thing, you have to prove or have probable cause for bias. That’s what makes it different.
But the sexual assault don’t need probable cause?

No, no, it’s just the motive doesn’t matter, right? In other words, if I’m looking at the sexual assault or any other crimes, we don’t– I mean, the motive does not matter as a legal issue, right? It’s a sexual assault, that’s it, whatever the motive might have been. But for a hate crime, whether it’s a hate crime turns on what the motive was. If the motive was anti-Jewish and we can prove it, that’s a hate

crime. If it’s something else entirely, then it’s not.
And that’s the reason for reporting them differently?
Well, that’s why we have–
[interposing] I’m asking you, because it’s not just making sense.

No, no, because you have these two different layers. Because the point is that you have this universe of crimes that come in, right, the reported hate crimes. And that’s going to be– so you’re talking about criminal– potential criminal conduct, right? We’re capturing that. But then a separate question– but one set is, hey, has a crime that has been reported to us that is under investigation as a hate crime, right? That’s one universe. Second universe, yes, we’ve confirmed that’s a hate crime. That distinction wouldn't make sense for other types of crimes. A sexual assault has been reported. Okay. that’s a sexual assault complaint. A murder has been reported, that’s it. To say, okay, it’s like a potential murder versus a

confirmed murder, that wouldn't make sense. It’s– again–
[interposing] But woudln’t it be possible that a sexual assault report is actually not confirmed because it was consensual?

So, that’s– so, different issue. We– to the extent we have– when we have crime data, we do all sorts of checks and audits, and there are times when things have been misclassified. That does happen, or we learn more. That’s to your point. But it’s all again, it’s a single question. Do we have a crime here? Right? And answer is binary, either we do or we don’t.

Understand why it needs to be reported differently. So, using sexual assault as an example, is sexual assault or allegations of sexual assault crimes reproted and displayed ot the public in a different way than hate crimes are? Meaning all of the ones that are just alleged, not confirmed. Are you reporting those as well?

So, any complaint that comes in of any type of crime, we’re going to take and record that as the crime that has

been described. It has to be classified in our system and we got to– and we’re checking. We have to make sure it’s classified properly. We’re taking those complaints, right? It could be sexual assault, murder. It could be larceny. Whatever it may be, and we’re tracking those complaints as they come in, and we report that data out in a variety of ways.
I’m just asking if you reported the reported incidents?
Yes, yes.
When it comes to sexual assault.
Yes.
And do you separate them in the same way that you do with hate crimes meaning you have one metric for recorded and one for confirmed or not do that?
No, because the reported versus for hate crimes is not whether there was a crime. It’s whether if there was a bias motive, and that bias motive question is unique to hate crimes.

I guess I just don’t understand why it still needs to be reported

differently, but it’s fine. We can move on. There’s been a lot of confusion about what is or isn’t a hate crime which may potentially lead to under-reporting. So, to clear this to the public, could you answer if you can, if the following would be classified as a hate crime, a bias incident, anti-semitic hate crime, or it’s just free speech? So, I’ll give you a couple of examples and if you can tell us I think that would clarify a lot for the public. So, for an example, protestors chanting outside a synagogue in support of Hamas. Hate crime, bias incident, free speech, whatever?
So, again, without more–
[interposing] Yeah.
I want to be clear without more, all you have is protestors outside of whatever the location is chanting in support of Hamas, no, that’s is protected speech. That’s free speech.
Okay.

I want to be– sorry, just to be clear. I want to emphasize I appreciate very, very well how painful and awful that

would be is for people inside let’s say that shule, I understand that. But the question is, is that a crime? No, it’s not. It’s protected speech.
Okay, and then protestors yelling outside of a synagogue at te Jews.

That is also protected speech. By the way, I’m assuming– again, I’m assuming no other facts. So, they’re not otherwise disrupting the services. They’re not obstructing anyone in any way, but simply the statement that you made, that is protected speech.
I mean, they are obstructing entrances to synagogues, is that–
[interposing] And they’re subject to arrest.
That is a hate crime?

No. So, it would be discon [sic]. Let me back up. If there are services going on, they’re obstructing from people going into services, there actually could very well be a hate crime. It’s going to depend a little bit on the circumstances. Any which way, if someone’s

blocking an entrance to a synagogue, they’re getting arrested, full stop.
What would be in that– in that fact pattern– in that fact pattern.-- in that fact pattern, what would be the circumstances that would make it a hate crime?

So, a few things. Certainly if you have any situation in which there’s a threat of harm, right– called a true threat in the first amendment right? So that threat situation, we would charge as an aggravated harassment. Right? Aggravated harassment, and we would charge that as a hate crime, assuming you could– well, you’d be able to show in that sort of situation. It’ll be charged as a hate crime. One thing also is there are particular statutes. They're not hate crime statutes. There are particular statutes about obstructing religious services. There’s a federal statute about obstructing, going into a house of worship. I mean, I think– I actually– I would characterize that as a hate crime statute, whether the federal government calls it that, that’s what it is. And so there’d be a charge there. For any kind of obstruction or threat, criminal in nature, and

again, I think on the circumstance it would get charged as a hate crime under a hate crime statute. But the speech, if that’s what you’re talking about, pure speech, whether that’s in support of Hamas or, you know, F the Jews I think was an example you gave, that is hurtful and painful, but in and of itself, that is protected speech.

Thank you very much. So, just to clarify, if there are protestors– let’s say there are mass protestors standing outside of a synagogue yelling at the Jews and obstructing the entrance, that is a hate crime?

No, so as I said, if they are obstructing an entrance, that is definitely a– you can’t do that. They’ll be warned, and if they refuse to move they’re subject to arrest, full stop. You know, how we charge that, under what statute we charge is going to depend a little bit on the circumstances, but they certainly are subject to arrest, no question about that. Whether they’ll be charged in the state, charged federally, how that would get prosecuted is going to depend on the circumstances and every case is different. But

you’re blocking an entrance to a synagogue or to a school, you are 100 percent subject to arrest.

And some other examples. Let’s say a kippah is being thrown off someone’s head. They’re walking on the street. Someone randomly comes over, throws off the kippah without saying anything, is that a hate crime?

So, that’s going to be charged essentially under the– what I would call a hate crime provision of the aggravated harassment statute. Aggravated harassment in the second degree actually has a special provision. If you’re knocking religious head gear off of someone, a kippah or otherwise– and that, I mean, it’s not the hate crime statute, but it is an enhancement. It is functionally the same thing, right? That is a provision of the aggravated harassment statute.
They’re subject to arrest?
Oh yeah, of course, and they’ll be charged as aggravated harassment in the second degree.

I mean, we’ve never seen– I’ve never seen, maybe I don’t know, but

any charges for cases like that. Maybe because it’s tough to find the perpetrator, but–
[interposing] We do have cases like that.
love to see these be prosecuted. Just a couple more. Someone on the train yelling “F you, Jew” or “dirty Jew” without any physical assault. Is that a hate crime?
